chapters.title: Chapter 5: Valuation and Fundamental Mean Reversion

lessons.title: Case Study: PSU Banks' Multi-Year Valuation Reversion

children.text: For the better part of a decade, India's public sector banks were the textbook example of an out-of-favor sector. Trading at steep discounts to book value for years, they were either the market's best-telegraphed rotation trade or the market's most patient value trap, and for most of that stretch, it was genuinely difficult to know which. This case study walks through what actually happened, and closes this chapter with an honest answer to the question it has been building toward: when the reversion finally came, was it mean reversion, a re-rating, or something in between?

body.text: PSU banks' journey from deep discount to broad re-rating was neither pure statistical mean reversion nor a pure structural re-rating in isolation. It was both, in sequence: a genuine cyclical low that took years to be confirmed by real fundamental evidence, followed by a re-rating to a new, healthier equilibrium that never simply returned to the sector's old, pre-crisis multiples.

children.text: The Setup: A Sector-Wide Valuation Collapse

The Reserve Bank of India's Asset Quality Review, beginning in 2015, forced banks to recognize years of understated bad loans on their books. Gross non-performing asset ratios across public sector banks, which had looked manageable, rose sharply as hidden stress came to light, pushing several large PSU banks toward reported losses. Price-to-book multiples across the sector, which had traded closer to their long-run average before the review, collapsed toward steep discounts as the market repriced the sector's genuine capital and asset-quality risk.

body.title: PSU Banks: A Decade in Five Milestones (approximate, rounded dates)

events.title: Asset Quality Review begins
events.description: The RBI forces recognition of previously understated bad loans across the banking sector, sharply raising reported gross NPA ratios at PSU banks.

events.title: Large government recapitalization announced
events.description: The government unveils a large bank recapitalization package, commonly cited at around ₹2.11 lakh crore, to shore up PSU banks' capital adequacy.

events.title: Mega-mergers consolidate the sector
events.description: Ten public sector banks are merged into four larger entities, a structural consolidation of the sector, effective from April 2020.

events.title: Covid-19 adds further pressure
events.description: The pandemic crash pressures an already-weak sector further, pushing valuation discounts to some of their widest levels.

events.title: A broad, multi-year re-rating
events.description: Gross NPA ratios decline meaningfully from their peak, credit growth and profitability improve, and PSU bank valuations re-rate substantially, though not uniformly back to pre-2015 levels.

children.text: The Discount Years: Cyclical Candidate or Value Trap?

Run Lesson 2's framework on the sector as it stood in, say, 2019. PSU banks were trading at a deep discount to book value. Gross NPA ratios were still elevated. A wave of mergers had just been announced, itself a signal of a sector under real, not imagined, stress. Applying the cyclical-vs-structural test honestly, the evidence available at the time was genuinely mixed. Bank credit cycles have turned before, repeatedly, across decades of Indian banking history, which supported the cyclical case. But the confirming evidence, NPA ratios actually declining, credit growth actually resuming, had not yet shown up. In real time, this was not an obvious call. It only looks obvious in hindsight.

body.title: PSU banking sector: illustrative price-to-book ratio, 2014 to 2024 (rounded, approximate)

children.text: The re-rating that followed was not confirmed by the stock price alone, prices rising is never itself evidence, as Chapter 1 established from the very first lesson. It was confirmed by gross NPA ratios genuinely declining from their peak as older bad loans were provided for, written off, or recovered, by credit growth resuming as banks became willing and able to lend again, and by improving profitability and return on equity as the cleaned-up loan books started generating healthier earnings. These were the same category of signal Lesson 2 pointed to for any cyclical sector: capacity, in this case lending capacity, actually turning, not merely a beaten-down price looking for a reason to bounce.

Look at the chart again. The sector's price-to-book ratio recovered dramatically off its trough, but it did not simply climb back to its 2014 level. It settled at a new, different level, still a genuine, substantial re-rating from the depths of 2020, but built on a materially different banking sector than the one that existed before 2015: better-capitalized after the recapitalization, structurally consolidated after the mergers, and carrying a cleaner loan book after years of recognition and provisioning. The honest answer to this chapter's question is that both things happened. Part of the move was a reversion of excess pessimism, once it became clear the worst of the bad-loan cycle had passed. Part of it was a genuine re-rating to a new equilibrium, because the sector itself was no longer the same sector it had been in 2014.

body.caption: The old mean vs the new equilibrium

cells: Substantially strengthened by the 2017 recap and years of retained earnings
Consolidated into four larger, post-merger entities
Recognized, provided for, and substantially cleaned up
The old average P/B is not the correct reversion target

body.text: This is the lesson this entire chapter has been building toward. A statistically justified discount and a genuinely improving fundamental picture are not competing explanations. They can both be true, one after the other, in the same sector, which is exactly why Chapter 1's fundamental check and Chapter 2's statistical toolkit were never meant to be used separately.

body.title: Compute a sector's valuation z-score
body.prompt: A bank sector's 10-year average price-to-book ratio is 1.1, with a standard deviation of 0.3. It is currently trading at 0.5x book. What is its valuation z-score?
body.explanation: (0.5 - 1.1) / 0.3 = -0.6 / 0.3 = -2.0. A reading this negative is statistically notable, exactly the kind of number that should prompt the cyclical-vs-structural investigation this case study just walked through, not an automatic buy signal on its own.

body.title: What actually confirmed the turnaround?
body.question: By around 2022, which development was the strongest evidence that PSU banks' earlier valuation discount reflected a turning credit cycle rather than a permanent structural problem?
options: PSU bank stock prices had already risen sharply, which alone proves the turnaround was real
Gross NPA ratios had declined meaningfully from their earlier peak, alongside improving credit growth and profitability
The stocks remained below their all-time highs, so there was automatically more room to run
Government ownership meant the sector was inherently risk-free
body.explanation: Genuine fundamental confirmation, declining NPA ratios, resuming credit growth, and improving profitability, is what validated the cyclical read, consistent with Lesson 2's framework. Price action alone, distance from an old high, and government ownership are all reasoning traps this course has warned against since Chapter 1: none of them are evidence of anything on their own.

points: PSU banks traded at steep valuation discounts for years following the RBI's 2015 Asset Quality Review, a genuine, sector-wide value collapse driven by newly recognized bad loans.

In real time, distinguishing this from a structural value trap was genuinely difficult until the confirming fundamental evidence, declining NPA ratios, resumed credit growth, improving profitability, actually appeared, years later.

The eventual re-rating was not a simple return to the sector's old, pre-2015 average valuation. It settled at a new equilibrium, reflecting a genuinely stronger, consolidated, better-capitalized banking sector.
This is the chapter's central lesson in one real case: a statistically justified discount and a genuine fundamental improvement are not competing explanations. Both were true here, in sequence.

This closes Chapter 5. Chapter 6 moves from single-asset valuation to the relationship between two assets, introducing pairs-based reversion and where this course hands off to the deeper statistical arbitrage toolkit.
